kp.k: Contractual incompleteness can arise without bounded rationality
kp.d: Hart and Moore develop a theoretical foundation for incomplete contracting, rather than empirical evidence about AI or legal-service transformation. Against the criticism that rational parties can overcome difficulties describing future trade through message-based mechanisms, they show that severe contractual incompleteness can remain optimal even when all possible trades can be described costlessly in advance.
qs: First, we develop a model, inspired by Segal (1995, 1998), in which it is costless to delineate the set of possible trades in advance
However, this result in no way undermines the conclusion that the optimal contract is incomplete.

kp.k: Observable information need not be enforceable information
kp.d: The model distinguishes what contracting parties observe from what courts can verify. A buyer and seller contract before relationship-specific investment and subsequent trade; they are risk neutral, unconstrained by wealth, and able to maximize expected payoffs. Exactly one of N widgets is appropriate in each state, with no natural quantity or quality ordering. Investments cannot themselves be specified enforceably, and the state and final payoffs cannot be observed by outsiders. These are modelling assumptions, not measured features of actual contracting.
qs: We assume that both parties observe the state of nature at date 1
However the state is not verifiable, and nor are the parties’ final payoffs: that is, these things cannot be observed by outsiders, such as the courts.
An important feature of our model, found also in Segal’s work, is that there is no natural metric or ordering on the good to be traded

kp.k: Commitment can restore efficient investment without advance descriptions
kp.d: Proposition 1 establishes that, in the basic seller-investment model, commitment not to renegotiate permits the first-best even when widgets cannot be described initially. Giving the seller a take-it-or-leave-it offer at the trading date lets her capture the surplus and internalize cost reductions. Hart and Moore recognize Maskin and Tirole’s broader commitment-based irrelevance theorem as an important contribution, while stressing its reliance on enforceable commitment.
qs: If the parties can commit not to renegotiate, then the first-best can be achieved.
This way S captures all the date 1 surplus, and, anticipating this, makes the efficient investment decision at date 1/2.

kp.k: Renegotiation undermines threats intended to support investment
kp.d: Without commitment, the buyer can reject the seller’s offer and bargain over the remaining gains from trade. Under the exposition’s assumption that the buyer has all renegotiation bargaining power, the buyer extracts the surplus and the seller has no incentive to invest. Renegotiation ensures efficient eventual trade but undermines the ex ante incentives that the original mechanism was intended to create.
qs: Under this assumption, the take-it-or-leave-it contract of Proposition 1 works very badly, because B can reject S’s offer and rely instead on bargaining to extract all the surplus, which gives S absolutely no incentive to invest at date 1/2 to reduce her expected costs.

kp.k: Rich trade possibilities make contracting asymptotically ineffective
kp.d: Proposition 2 shows that, with no commitment, symmetric uncertainty across widget identities, and generic-widget costs densely spanning the relevant range, every contract approaches the null contract’s investment outcome as N grows. In the buyer-bargaining-power case, seller investment approaches zero. Renegotiation makes contractual outcomes too similar across states to screen cost realizations effectively. The result is asymptotic, not a claim that every finite contract is worthless; gaps in the generic cost range can instead support positive investment.
qs: The surprising fact is that, for large N, no other contract can do significantly better!
That is, in the limit, contracts cannot make any difference to expected total surplus, and the parties may as well use the null contract.
Clearly, for the purpose of mechanism design, adding a constant to one of the parties’ payoffs does not help screen the states.

kp.k: The null-contract result extends beyond one-sided investment
kp.d: The appendix generalizes the limiting result to both parties investing, potentially in multiple dimensions, and to any division of subsequent bargaining surplus. It permits investment externalities and correlation between buyer value and seller cost, subject to boundedness and symmetry assumptions and a unique null-contract investment equilibrium. Investments converge to that equilibrium, not necessarily to zero: zero investment is specific to the simpler seller-only case with all bargaining power assigned to the buyer.
qs: In this Appendix we generalise Proposition 2 to the case where both parties make investments
Also, we allow for any division of surplus in the date 1 bargaining.
But this means that, up to an additive constant, the expected price paid by B to S is the same as if the parties bargained from scratch at date 1

kp.k: Advance describability matters when commitment is unavailable
kp.d: The authors reject a general interpretation that descriptions never matter. In an extension where the special widget’s identity is known beforehand, a describable widget supports a fixed-price specific-performance contract and first-best investment. Without an advance vocabulary identifying it, contracting remains approximately equivalent to the null contract. They explain that Maskin and Tirole’s Theorem 4 requires maximality and renegotiation welfare neutrality; adding rare fringe states can satisfy maximality while preserving the example’s force, leaving welfare neutrality as the restrictive condition.
qs: The inability to describe the widgets ex ante can make a big difference.
Their result requires two conditions: first, that the set of states is "maximal"; and, second, that the final outcome is “renegotiation welfare neutral."
nondescribability is generally an important constraint in the absence of a commitment not to renegotiate.

kp.k: Partial specification can improve investment without achieving efficiency
kp.d: An extension introduces M defined widgets among N possibilities, with N large relative to M. Investment reduces costs across the defined category but has a greater effect on the special widget. A fixed-price contract restricting delivery to that category supports positive investment below the first-best and is asymptotically optimal as M grows. Either party may choose the widget, or it may be specified initially. The category is exogenous, so this is not a model of choosing incompleteness continuously; without advance describability, investment again approaches zero as N and N/M grow.
qs: However, there is more investment than under the null contract:

In the limit, it is optimal to contract for the delivery of one of the defined widgets at a fixed price; the particular widget may be chosen by B or S at date 1, or may be specified in advance at date 0.
the set of defined widgets is exogenously given.

kp.k: Legal and institutional constraints complicate renegotiation prohibitions
kp.d: Hart and Moore argue that parties can cancel irrevocability clauses or waive renegotiation penalties through a new contract under the legal system they discuss. They report Maskin and Tirole’s proposed registration system that would prioritize the original contract, but question its institutional feasibility and effectiveness. Indirect trades through middlemen could circumvent prohibitions, and courts might struggle to distinguish circumvention from legitimate transactions. These are the authors’ institutional arguments, not an empirical evaluation of legal regimes.
qs: The point is that the courts will enforce the hew contract rather than the original one.
However, a registration system like this does not exist anywhere in the world as far as we know, and would require a system-wide institutional change.

There may be quite legitimate sequences of trade linking S to B through various middlemen, and it may be hard for a judge to distinguish between the legitimate ones and the ones that are designed to circumvent a “no renegotiation” provision.

kp.k: Third-party penalties improve incentives but invite collusion
kp.d: The authors construct a three-party mechanism achieving first-best investment despite renegotiation by separating a buyer’s penalty from a seller’s reward. They then show that side deals returning fines to a contracting party can destroy those incentives. They also question proposals to pay fines to the public because of enforcement, representation, and collection problems. Their suggestion that the null-contract result could survive third parties with a continuum of widgets is explicitly a conjecture awaiting further research.
qs: Third parties can drive a wedge between B’s and S’s payoffs: B can be penalized without rewarding S, and vice versa.
Even if we stick to the case of a finite number of generic widgets, the above contract is vulnerable to collusion.
We conjecture that in some properly articulated model with a continuum of widgets, the conclusions of Proposition 2 will hold, even allowing for third parties; but this awaits further research.

kp.k: Lottery penalties face insurance and manipulation trade-offs
kp.d: Hart and Moore examine Maskin and Tirole’s proposal to replace third-party fines with risky transfers when the buyer is at least slightly risk averse. They argue that objective randomness can be insured against, neutralizing its incentive effect, while private randomization may be manipulated. Endogenous randomization also raises opportunities to renegotiate before the uncertainty is resolved. They ultimately treat the feasibility of commitment as an unresolved issue on which reasonable analysts can disagree.
qs: the more objective a lottery is, the less it can be manipulated, but the more it can be insured against; the less objective a lottery is, the less it can be insured against, but the more it can be manipulated.
the degree of commitment is something about which reasonable people can disagree.

kp.k: Ownership improves investment by changing outside options
kp.d: The property-rights extension gives the seller access to the buyer’s downstream technology through ownership of nonhuman assets, but not the buyer’s specialized human capital. If independent downstream production is viable in both cost states, seller ownership restores first-best investment; if viable only in the low-cost state, it improves investment without eliminating underinvestment. The mechanism is the seller’s improved fallback payoff rather than a change in assumed bargaining power.
qs: We will assume that, as owner, S has residual rights of control over B’s assets, in the sense that S has access to B’s downstream technology.
The conclusion so far is that a reallocation of property rights can help when contracts are incomplete.

kp.k: Ownership predictions remain qualified and theoretically incomplete
kp.d: The authors accept Maskin and Tirole’s observation that joint ownership with a sale option can reproduce seller ownership’s second-best outcome, while arguing that this does not eliminate predictive content. They find the option mechanism fragile to uncertainty in independent downstream value and conjecture that uncertainty could reduce ownership indeterminacy. They also acknowledge that their model equates residual rights with complete control and does not yet formally derive ownership from the distinction between describable and hard-to-describe asset uses.
qs: there may be more than one allocation of property rights that sustains the second-best optimum.
In fact, we conjecture that the indeterminacy in optimal ownership structure will be much reduced, and may disappear, in a world of uncertainty.
the above analysis falls some way short of providing a fully satisfactory foundation for a theory of ownership.

kp.k: Incompleteness means insufficient contingency, not necessarily missing obligations
kp.d: The paper distinguishes contracts with omissions or ambiguities from contracts that fully specify obligations but cannot incorporate desired state-contingent terms. Its optimal contracts belong to the latter category: even the null contract clearly assigns no obligations. Subsequent renegotiation supplies contingent terms and efficient trade, but its allocation of payoffs can remain inferior from the ex ante investment perspective. The authors acknowledge that the terminology is partly semantic while defending the distinction from traditional comprehensive contracting.
qs: The null contract is complete in that it is absolutely clear what everybody’s obligations are: nobody has any!
it is incomplete if the parties would like to add contingent clauses, but are prevented from doing so by the fact that the state of nature cannot be verified
The parties would like to ensure that the price of the special widget is independent of S’s cost, but, as we have seen, this may not be compatible with their ex post incentive constraints.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Hart and Moore make claims about incomplete contracting and property rights, not AI: contractual incompleteness can arise even when describing possible trades is costless.
pts.d: In their baseline model, when parties cannot commit not to renegotiate and the set of possible trades becomes sufficiently rich, no contract appreciably improves investment incentives over the null contract. In the main-text case where the buyer has all renegotiation bargaining power, seller investment approaches zero. The appendix generalizes the result to both parties investing and arbitrary divisions of bargaining power: investments approach their null-contract levels, not necessarily zero. The authors also demonstrate that describability matters in extensions, that partially incomplete contracts can improve investment without attaining first-best, and that reallocating asset ownership can alleviate underinvestment. These are cross-domain theoretical claims, not predictions about legal technology.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of formal economic models, propositions, proofs and constructed examples, rather than empirical observations.
pts.d: Proposition 1 establishes first-best implementation with commitment not to renegotiate. Proposition 2 establishes the limiting null-contract result without commitment; the appendix extends it to multidimensional investments, investment externalities and general bargaining shares. Proposition 3 establishes a limiting result for partially incomplete contracts. Section 4 uses a stylized ownership model to show how access to downstream assets changes the seller's outside option and investment incentives. The commitment discussion offers institutional reasoning about renegotiation, side-contracting, collusion and insurance, not systematic legal or empirical evidence. The authors explicitly label some further claims as conjectures, including the survival of the null-contract result with a continuum of widgets and third parties, and reduced indeterminacy of ownership under uncertainty.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The results concern a stylized contracting sequence and limiting model conditions, not a calendar forecast.
pts.d: Parties contract at date 0, invest between contracting and trade, and trade at date 1. The baseline assumes risk-neutral, unconstrained, rational parties; states and payoffs observable to the parties but not verifiable by courts; investment that cannot be specified enforceably; equally likely permutations of widget identities; and generic-widget costs densely covering the relevant range as their number increases. Lack of commitment not to renegotiate is crucial: with commitment, the main-text model can attain first-best even without ex ante describability. The authors qualify their account of partial incompleteness because the set of defined widgets is exogenous. Their ownership analysis is preliminary, and they acknowledge that it does not fully distinguish residual from specific control rights. In this paper, legal verifiability concerns what courts can observe, not human checking of AI output.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected actors are contracting buyers and sellers, investing firms, asset owners and potential third-party participants—not identified legal-service market segments.
pts.d: The seller's investment incentives weaken when renegotiation transfers the benefits of cost reduction to the buyer. More generally, both parties' investment incentives depend on their bargaining shares. Partial contracts can preserve some incentive to invest, while downstream asset ownership can improve the seller's fallback payoff and sometimes restore first-best incentives. Buyers and sellers jointly face lower expected total surplus from underinvestment, even though renegotiation ensures efficient trade after the state is realized. Courts enter as enforcement institutions constrained by unverifiable information; third parties can create incentive-enhancing penalties but may collude with a contracting party. The source makes no claims about AI-related effects on lawyers, law firms, legal departments or access to justice.
